title: Trump Sells Advanced F-35 Fighter Jets to UAE as Abraham Accords Side Deal
description_short: Trump Sells Advanced F-35 Fighter Jets to UAE as Abraham Accords Side Deal
description_medium: In November 2020, the Trump administration advanced a proposed arms package for the United Arab Emirates that included up to 50 F-35 stealth fighters, armed drones, and other weapons, with an estimated value of $23 billion. The sale followed the UAE-Israel Abraham Accords and raised concerns about Israel’s U.S.-backed qualitative military edge. The Biden administration later paused the transaction for review; the aircraft were not delivered as part of this announcement.
description_long: The Trump administration agreed to pursue a sale of up to 50 advanced F-35 fighters to the United Arab Emirates, along with armed drones and other weapons, in a package valued at about $23 billion. The proposal followed the UAE’s normalization agreement with Israel, known as the Abraham Accords, and was presented as part of the diplomatic opening. It raised concerns in Israel because longstanding U.S. policy had sought to preserve Israel’s qualitative military edge over neighboring states. Israeli officials reportedly lobbied privately against the arms transfer even as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu publicly praised the accords. title: Taj Mahal Collapses: Trump's First Bankruptcy and $675 Million Junk Bond Disaster
description_short: Taj Mahal Collapses: Trump's First Bankruptcy and $675 Million Junk Bond Disaster
description_medium: The Trump Taj Mahal casino filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection on July 17, 1991, about 15 months after opening. description_long: On July 17, 1991, Trump Taj Mahal — billed as the world's largest casino at a construction cost of $1 billion — filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection just 15 months after its grand opening in April 1990. The casino had been financed with $675 million in junk bonds at a crushing 14 percent interest rate, a debt load so severe the property could not generate enough cash flow to service it even at peak revenues. As part of the reorganization plan, Trump surrendered 50 percent ownership of the casino to bondholders in exchange for a reduced interest rate of 11.35 percent. The bankruptcy was the first of six Trump entities to seek Chapter 11 protection over the following two decades, and exposed the fundamental hollowness of Trump's self-promoted image as a master dealmaker. Hundreds of small contractors and suppliers who had built and stocked the casino were paid cents on the dollar or nothing at all.

title: Cover-Up Certified: Judge Permanently Blocks Release of Mar-a-Lago Classified Documents Report
description_short: Cover-Up Certified: Judge Permanently Blocks Release of Mar-a-Lago Classified Documents Report
description_medium: On February 23, 2026, Judge Aileen Cannon permanently barred the Justice Department from releasing Special Counsel Jack Smith’s report on the Mar-a-Lago classified-documents case. description_long: On February 23, 2026, Florida federal judge Aileen Cannon — Trump's own 2020 appointee — permanently barred the Justice Department from releasing Special Counsel Jack Smith's report on Trump's illegal retention of classified documents at Mar-a-Lago, calling its release a manifest injustice. Smith's two-volume report detailed how Trump stored documents related to nuclear programs, defense capabilities, foreign intelligence, and potential military vulnerabilities at his private club, which hosted hundreds of paying members and foreign nationals. Trump had been indicted on 37 federal counts before Cannon dismissed the case in 2024 on the grounds that Smith was not lawfully appointed. The documents — over 300 records with classified markings — included material on nuclear weapons programs and signals intelligence so sensitive that their compromise could cause irreplaceable loss of technical or human access that took years and significant resources to develop. In the second term, rather than implementing stronger security protocols at Mar-a-Lago, Trump continued using the club as a de facto second White House, and no damage assessment was ever publicly released.

title: Flag Burning Criminalization - Defying Supreme Court Rulings
description_short: Flag Burning Criminalization - Defying Supreme Court Rulings
description_medium: In August 2025, Trump signed an executive order directing federal prosecutors to pursue cases related to flag burning and threatening jail time for people who burned the U.S. flag. The order challenged the Supreme Court’s 1989 ruling in Texas v. Johnson, which treats flag burning as protected symbolic speech. The directive did not itself overturn that precedent or make protected expression a valid crime.
description_long: Donald Trump signed an executive order attempting to criminalize flag burning and impose one-year jail sentences for the constitutionally protected form of political protest, openly defying the Supreme Court's 1989 ruling in Texas v. Johnson that established flag burning as symbolic speech protected under the First Amendment. Trump declared 'If you burn a flag, you get one year in jail, no early exits, no nothing. And it goes on your record and you'll see flag burning stop immediately' while directing Attorney General Pam Bondi to 'vigorously prosecute' flag burners. The order represented an unprecedented presidential attempt to criminalize constitutionally protected expression through executive decree, with Trump claiming without evidence that 'foreign nationals are using flag burning to intimidate and threaten American citizens.' The Foundation for Individual Rights in Education warned that 'Trump may think he has the power to override the First Amendment with the stroke of a pen, but he doesn't,' emphasizing that 'the government can't criminalize protected expressive activity.' The executive order attempted to sidestep the Supreme Court precedent by directing prosecution for 'related crimes' during flag burning incidents, while threatening visa revocation and deportation for foreign nationals who engage in the protected political expression. Free speech organizations called the order a dangerous precedent that could lead to criminalizing other forms of political protest, with Trump's defiance of established constitutional law representing an authoritarian rejection of judicial authority over executive power.

title: Trump Claims He Invented the Word 'Prime' (as in Prime the Pump)
description_short: Trump Claims He Invented the Word 'Prime' (as in Prime the Pump)
description_medium: During a May 2017 interview with The Economist, Donald Trump said he had never heard the phrase “prime the pump” before and believed he had coined it. He asked the interviewer to confirm that it was new. Merriam-Webster noted that the expression had appeared in print as early as 1933, decades before the interview.
description_long: In an interview with The Economist published on May 11, 2017, Trump discussed “prime the pump,” a phrase for government spending intended to stimulate economic activity. He said he had not heard it before and claimed he had coined it days earlier, pressing the interviewer to confirm that it was a new expression. Merriam-Webster responded that the phrase had been in use since at least 1933. The exchange quickly became a widely repeated example of Trump claiming credit for familiar language. The dictionary’s history directly contradicted the claim that the phrase was new, though it could not establish whether Trump knew of its earlier use. The moment was small compared with his economic policy proposals, but it illustrated how a readily checkable historical fact could challenge a public claim made during an interview. The discussion centered on the phrase’s origin, not on whether the spending policy Trump described would work.

title: U.S. Drops to 57th on 2025 World Press Freedom Index
description_short: U.S. Drops to 57th on 2025 World Press Freedom Index
description_medium: Reporters Without Borders ranked the United States 57th of 180 countries in its 2025 World Press Freedom Index, a two-place drop from 2024. RSF also downgraded the country’s status from satisfactory to problematic and reported a decline of more than 14 points in the economic indicator over two years. The organization attributed broader deterioration to conditions facing journalists and news outlets.
description_long: On May 2, 2025, Reporters Without Borders (RSF) published its 2025 World Press Freedom Index, ranking the United States 57th out of 180 countries — a drop of two additional places from its 2024 ranking, extending a slide of over 25 places in recent years. The U.S. now ranked one position behind Sierra Leone and was downgraded from satisfactory to problematic in press freedom status. RSF stated that Donald Trump's second term as president has led to an alarming deterioration in press freedom, indicative of an authoritarian shift in government. The economic indicator for U.S. press freedom had fallen more than 14 points in two years. Over 60 percent of journalists surveyed in Arizona, Florida, Nevada, and Pennsylvania said it was difficult to earn a living wage as a journalist, and 75 percent said their outlet struggles for economic viability. The U.S. Press Freedom Tracker recorded more than 170 attacks on journalists in 2025 — nearly double the previous year — driven by increased violence at protests and law enforcement confrontations. RSF cited Trump's efforts to censor government data, dismantle public broadcasters, weaponize regulatory agencies, halt international media freedom aid, and sue disfavored outlets as the primary drivers of the decline.

title: Taj Mahal Collapses: Trump's First Bankruptcy and $675 Million Junk Bond Disaster
description_short: Taj Mahal Collapses: Trump's First Bankruptcy and $675 Million Junk Bond Disaster
description_medium: The Trump Taj Mahal casino filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection on July 17, 1991, about 15 months after opening. The property had been financed with $675 million in high-interest junk bonds. Under the reorganization, Trump gave bondholders a 50 percent ownership stake in exchange for a lower interest rate, shifting part of the loss to investors and suppliers.
description_long: On July 17, 1991, Trump Taj Mahal — billed as the world's largest casino at a construction cost of $1 billion — filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection just 15 months after its grand opening in April 1990. The casino had been financed with $675 million in junk bonds at a crushing 14 percent interest rate, a debt load so severe the property could not generate enough cash flow to service it even at peak revenues. As part of the reorganization plan, Trump surrendered 50 percent ownership of the casino to bondholders in exchange for a reduced interest rate of 11.35 percent. The bankruptcy was the first of six Trump entities to seek Chapter 11 protection over the following two decades, and exposed the fundamental hollowness of Trump's self-promoted image as a master dealmaker. Hundreds of small contractors and suppliers who had built and stocked the casino were paid cents on the dollar or nothing at all.

title: Deutsche Bank Laundered $10B+ in Russian Money — Trump's Primary Lender
description_short: Deutsche Bank Laundered $10B+ in Russian Money — Trump's Primary Lender
description_medium: In 2017, U.S. and U.K. regulators penalized Deutsche Bank over “mirror trades” that moved about $10 billion from Russia into Western markets. The bank was also a major lender to Donald Trump. Congressional investigators sought Trump’s bank records, but the available reporting does not show that money from the trades reached his loans or accounts.
description_long: Between 2011 and 2015, Deutsche Bank’s so-called mirror trades moved Russian money into Western financial markets by pairing purchases of Russian securities in rubles with sales of matching securities in London for dollars. U.S. and British regulators later penalized the bank for anti-money-laundering failures connected to the trades. New York’s Department of Financial Services imposed a $425 million penalty; total U.S. and U.K. penalties were reported at about $630 million. During the same period, Deutsche Bank was one of Donald Trump’s major lenders. Congressional investigators sought Trump’s bank records to examine the relationship, and the bank initially resisted disclosure. The overlap between the bank’s money-laundering case and its lending to Trump drew scrutiny, but no evidence establishes that proceeds from the trades reached Trump’s loans or accounts. The regulatory case and the bank’s lending relationship were separate matters. The allegations against the bank do not establish that Trump participated in its scheme.

description_short: Military Force Threats Against Domestic Political Opposition
description_medium: During the 2024 campaign, Trump said he might use the military against people he called “the enemy from within” and discussed military action for other domestic and foreign policy goals. title: Trump Retaliates Against Brad Raffensperger and Election Officials Who Refused to Overturn 2020
description_short: Trump Retaliates Against Brad Raffensperger and Election Officials Who Refused to Overturn 2020
description_medium: In March 2025, Trump said people he blamed for the 2020 election “should go to jail” and later directed the Justice Department to review former CISA director Chris Krebs. Brennan Center coverage describes administration threats of prosecution against election officials. The claims about later Georgia party actions, an endorsement, and a 2026 bomb scare require separate documentation.
description_long: Throughout 2025 and 2026, Trump and his DOJ constructed an apparatus of retaliation against officials who had certified the 2020 election. In a March 14, 2025 speech, Trump stated: What a difference a rigged and crooked election had on our country. And the people who did this to us should go to jail. An executive order directed DOJ to review the actions of Chris Krebs — Trump's own CISA director — because he denied that the 2020 election was rigged and stolen. The Georgia GOP's June 2025 convention passed a resolution calling for the party to block Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger from qualifying on the Republican ticket for daring to certify Biden's 2020 win. Trump endorsed Raffensperger's opponent Burt Jones — one of the fake electors — for governor. On May 13, 2026, Raffensperger's gubernatorial campaign reported an active threat and a bomb scare at a campaign event; Raffensperger said: When you stand on principle, some people will hate you, even want to try and hurt you. The Brennan Center documented that the administration's threats of prosecution were designed to ensure that election officials facing future pressure would capitulate rather than risk the retaliation Raffensperger endured for doing his job.
